aliases.name: Hopping vampire
aliases.meaning: Western popular term for the jiangshi

description.summary: The jiangshi (僵尸, 'stiff corpse') is a reanimated corpse from Chinese folklore, depicted in modern popular culture in Qing dynasty official garb, hopping with arms outstretched, and draining the qi (life force) of the living. It is repelled by Taoist talismans, mirrors, and other ritual implements.
description.full: The jiangshi (Mandarin jiāngshī, Cantonese goengsi) is a class of undead in Chinese folk religion and yokai-like popular folklore. The body is rigid (literally 'stiff corpse'), unable to bend at the knees, and so moves by hopping with arms thrust forward. Modern depictions standardize a Qing dynasty (1644–1912) court official's costume and a yellow paper talisman (符 fú) pasted to the forehead by a Taoist priest to control or pacify the corpse. Jiangshi are not blood-drinkers in the European sense but drain qi (氣) — vital breath / life force — from victims. Classical Qing-era literary sources are central: Yuan Mei's 'Zibuyu' (子不語, 'What the Master Would Not Discuss', 1788) and Ji Yun (Ji Xiaolan)'s 'Yuewei Caotang Biji' (閱微草堂筆記, 'Notes from the Thatched Cottage of Subtle Perception', late 18th century) catalogue jiangshi types and prevention methods. A widely-cited folk-cultural origin is the Xiangxi (Western Hunan) practice of 'transporting corpses over a thousand li' (赶尸 gǎnshī), in which Taoist priests reportedly led lines of corpses back to their hometowns for burial; observers describing this practice may have generated the modern hopping-corpse imagery. The jiangshi was made a global popular-culture icon by the 1985 Hong Kong horror-comedy 'Mr. Vampire' (殭屍先生), directed by Ricky Lau and produced by Sammo Hung, which spawned a sequel franchise and decades of related films, manhua, and video games. Defenses listed in folk and literary sources include peach-wood swords, sticky rice, mirrors, the blood of a black dog, the hooves of a black donkey, and Taoist talismans.

features.description: Modern depictions show jiangshi in Qing-era court / official dress with a round-topped, broad-brimmed hat
Yellow paper talisman bearing Taoist seal characters affixed to the forehead to bind or control the corpse
Arms held rigidly forward at shoulder height while moving
Long, often green or white-tipped, claw-like fingernails
Wild, white or grey hair, sometimes prematurely white

physical.morphology: Bipedal humanoid corpse, rigor-mortis stiffened so that the knees cannot bend, requiring locomotion by hopping. Body is described as a corpse in arrested decay rather than a living being.

abilities.description: Drains qi / vital breath from the living, often through breathing on or biting victims
Moves by stiff-legged hops, arms extended for balance
In folk and literary sources, jiangshi possess the strength of an enraged corpse
Locate victims by their breath; holding one's breath is a folk defense

behavior.diet: Qi (life force) of the living; classical sources do not emphasize blood specifically
patterns: Active at night; weak in sunlight
Driven by hunger for qi rather than malice in some accounts
Bound or pacified by Taoist priests (道士 dàoshi)

range.description: Native to Han Chinese folklore, with strong regional roots in southern China (especially Western Hunan / Xiangxi). The jiangshi spread throughout the Sinosphere — Hong Kong, Taiwan, Vietnam, Korea, and Japan — primarily through Hong Kong cinema in the 1980s.

hotspots.name: Xiangxi (Western Hunan)

location.description: Mountainous prefecture in western Hunan province, famed for the 'corpse-driving' (赶尸 gǎnshī) tradition

hotspots.notes: Cultural source of the modern 'hopping corpse' imagery via the corpse-transport tradition

peak_activity_periods.description: Classical literary cataloguing of jiangshi types
Hong Kong cinema 'jiangshi boom' anchored by the 'Mr. Vampire' franchise

temporal.seasonal_patterns: Folk tradition associates jiangshi activity with the seventh lunar month (Ghost Month)

origins.cultural_roots: Han Chinese folk religion and Taoist eschatology; beliefs about improper burial, restless corpses, and the necessity of returning bones to the ancestral home.
origins.earliest_accounts: Folk tradition predates surviving texts; the canonical literary catalogue is in Yuan Mei's 'Zibuyu' (1788) and Ji Yun's 'Yuewei Caotang Biji' (late 18th century).
origins.folklore_connections: Linked to the Xiangxi corpse-driving tradition (赶尸); to Taoist exorcism practice; and (in 20th-century pop culture) loosely conflated with the European vampire.

timeline.event: Yuan Mei publishes 'Zibuyu' (子不語), a major Qing-era anomaly-tale collection cataloguing jiangshi types and lore
Ji Yun's 'Yuewei Caotang Biji' (閱微草堂筆記) begins serial publication, including jiangshi tales and prevention methods
timeline.significance: Second pillar of the classical jiangshi corpus

timeline.event: Hong Kong release of 'Mr. Vampire' (殭屍先生), directed by Ricky Lau and produced by Sammo Hung
timeline.significance: Global mainstreaming of the jiangshi image and aesthetic

timeline.event: Taiwanese-produced children's TV series 'Hello Jacky / Hsin Jiangshi Xiansheng' (新殭屍先生), spreads the 'Kyonshī' boom across East Asia
timeline.significance: Children's-media propagation of jiangshi across the Sinosphere and Japan

history.modern_era: After the 1980s Hong Kong cinema 'jiangshi boom', the figure has continued to anchor East Asian horror-comedy, video games (Darkstalkers' Hsien-Ko, 1994), manhua, animation, and the vibrant cosplay / Halloween presence of the 'hopping vampire' across the Sinosphere.

documentary.name: Zibuyu (子不語) by Yuan Mei
documentary.description: Qing-era anomaly-tale collection containing extensive jiangshi taxonomy and lore.
documentary.analysis: Authoritative classical source; widely cited in folkloric and historical scholarship.

documentary.name: Yuewei Caotang Biji (閱微草堂筆記) by Ji Yun
documentary.description: Notes from the Thatched Cottage of Subtle Perception; major source on jiangshi prevention and case histories.
documentary.analysis: Second canonical Qing-era source on jiangshi.

paranormal.name: Folk-religious doctrine: improper burial and restless qi
paranormal.description: In Chinese folk religion, the dead must be buried at the ancestral home with proper rites, or the po-soul may animate the corpse as a jiangshi; the Xiangxi corpse-transport tradition is partly an explicit response to this danger.
evidence_cited: Classical literary sources (Yuan Mei, Ji Yun)

skeptical.name: Xiangxi corpse-driving misperception
skeptical.description: The modern 'hopping corpse' image likely derives from the Xiangxi practice in which Taoist priests bound corpses to long bamboo poles and walked them back to their home villages; observers seeing the procession at night, with corpses jolting as the bamboo flexed, plausibly produced the hopping-vampire imagery.
proponents: J. J. M. de Groot (Dutch sinologist, late 19th century)
evidence_cited: Geographic clustering of hopping-corpse motif in southern China

skeptical.name: Postmortem rigor and decomposition misinterpretation
skeptical.description: Folkloric jiangshi descriptions are consistent with cultural interpretation of normal postmortem rigor mortis, livor mortis (greenish discoloration), and natural sounds of decomposition.
evidence_cited: Description of jiangshi as 'stiff' and unable to bend

stories: Ji Yun 'Yuewei Caotang Biji' jiangshi tales (c. 1789–1798)
Folk anecdotes of Taoist priests pacifying jiangshi with talismans
folklore.beliefs: Belief in literal jiangshi has receded in modern urban China but remains a recognizable folk-religious framework; the figure is a fully entrenched cultural icon throughout the Sinosphere.
